title: A projection-free approach toward mapping the structured polarization fields
abstract: We present a projection-free method for mapping two-dimensional polarization distributions using Hong-Ou -Mandel (HOM) interference. Conventional polarization characterization techniques, such as Stokes polarimetry, rely on sequential intensity measurements under multiple polarization projections, making their accuracy and sensitivity susceptible to the extinction ratio, calibration errors, and stability of the polarization analysis optics. Our approach overcomes these limitations by exploiting the sensitivity of two-photon bunching to polarization indistinguishability at a balanced beam splitter. Using a HOM interferometer driven by a high-brightness spontaneous parametric down-conversion photon-pair source at 810 nm, we introduced a birefringent vortex waveplate with spatially varying polarization rotations in one interferometer arm and measured the resulting coincidence counts with a high signal-to-noise ratio, enabling projection-free characterization of the sample-induced polarization transformations. This configuration maps spatially dependent polarization variations directly onto coincidence counts, providing a projection-free reconstruction of the polarization distribution. We demonstrate high-fidelity ($\sim$95$\%$) reconstruction of the spatial polarization pattern with an angular resolution of approximately $\sim0.4^\circ$. The use an estimator that saturates the Cramer-Rao bound, computed from the Fisher information, can improve resolution further at the cost of longer acquisition. The proposed quantum-optical technique offers a simple, scalable, and high-precision framework for characterizing structured polarization fields in birefringent materials.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, high-precision technique for mapping polarization fields by utilizing Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference with entangled photon pairs. By measuring coincidence counts instead of performing multiple intensity projections, the method overcomes systematic errors inherent in traditional polarimetry. This provides a simple and scalable quantum-optical tool for characterizing structured birefringence.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a projection-free method for accurately mapping two-dimensional polarization distributions within structured materials.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that the coincidence counts from Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference can directly reconstruct the spatial polarization pattern with high fidelity ($\sim$95%).
method: They exploit the sensitivity of two-photon bunching to polarization indistinguishability at a balanced beam splitter, bypassing conventional projection measurements.
model_or_system: The experiment uses HOM interferometry driven by a spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) photon-pair source. The system involves analyzing coincidence counts ($P_c$) as a function of the sample's polarization transformation.
key_observables: Coincidence counts ($N_c$), which are mapped to the local polarization orientation ($	heta$) and fast-axis orientation map ($\phi$).
important_parameters: High coincidence-to-accidental ratio (CAR), angular resolution ($\sim 0.4^\circ$), and interference visibility ($\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the use of high-brightness sources for rapid acquisition, and theoretical derivations rely on approximations like narrow-bandpass Gaussian filters.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how coincidence counts change with polarization angle relative to the signal photon's initial polarization, showing characteristic dips/peaks used for reconstruction.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the limitations of conventional polarimetry (Stokes) to introducing the quantum-optical HOM technique. It details the theoretical dependence of $P_c$ on polarization indistinguishability and concludes with experimental demonstration of mapping structured fields.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics, as it uses fundamental quantum interference phenomena (HOM) to perform complex characterization tasks in a non-destructive, projection-free manner.
